support_text: The paper concludes that a principal role of ketamine in COVID-19 cholangiopathy cannot be proved by the case series and clinical trials conducted so far, nor is it supported by the radiological and histological features of post-COVID-19 secondary sclerosing cholangitis (SSC). It notes, however, that given its potential toxic effect on the biliary tree, ketamine can represent an additional precipitating factor in the disease pathogenesis.
qualifying_conditions: Principal causal role specifically in post-COVID-19 secondary sclerosing cholangitis is negated; paper leaves open that ketamine may be an additional precipitating factor; co-suspects include biliary ischemia, direct viral damage, toxic bile, and hyperinflammation.
extra_details: High-dose ketamine used to sedate severe COVID-19 ICU patients with factors altering drug metabolism (e.g., renal failure) that could contribute to drug precipitation in the biliary tract; in Butikofer et al. COVID-19 patients were more severe than influenza patients; in Ghafoor et al. only one-third of patients who developed post-COVID-19 SSC received ketamine; potential contribution via cholangiopathy resembling KIC (enzyme peak gradually reduced and dilated CBD after cessation in the Knooihuizen case report).

support_text: Ketamine undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, and although short-term use has been infrequently associated with elevated liver function tests, the paper explicitly states that clinically apparent liver damage has not been reported. Supporting observations include Dundee et al. finding significant liver-function elevations in 14 of 34 patients given 3-4 mg/kg ketamine for anesthesia, and a randomized trial by Noppers et al. in which 3 of 6 patients re-exposed to ketamine 16 days after a 100-hour infusion (mean dose 1813 mg) developed elevations ≥3 times baseline that returned to normal within 3 months. Approximately 10% of individuals receiving high-dose ketamine infusions experience significant liver-enzyme increases, yet no adverse hepatic effects were reported in a 60-patient CRPS RCT (average dose 22 mg/h over ~4.2 days).
qualifying_conditions: Negative claim pertains specifically to clinically apparent liver damage; isolated elevations in liver enzymes/transaminases are reported but are not characterized as clinically apparent drug-related liver injury.
extra_details: Short-term use infrequently associated with elevated liver function tests. Dundee et al.: 14 of 34 patients receiving 3-4 mg/kg ketamine for anesthesia had significant liver-function elevations. Noppers et al. RCT: 3 of 6 patients re-exposed to ketamine 16 days after a 100-hour infusion (max 0.4 mg/kg/h, mean dose 1813 mg) developed ≥3 times baseline liver-enzyme elevations that normalized within 3 months; the other two groups showed no abnormal liver tests. Approximately 10% of high-dose ketamine infusion recipients develop significant liver-enzyme increases. No adverse hepatic effects in a 60-patient CRPS RCT with continuous ketamine infusion (average 22 mg/h, ~4.2 days). The paper concludes there is insufficient evidence supporting routine preinfusion liver testing before IV ketamine in healthy individuals, but suggests case-by-case baseline/postinfusion LFTs for those with liver dysfunction, at risk of hepatotoxicity (e.g., alcohol abusers, chronic hepatitis), or receiving high frequent doses (grade C, low certainty).
